specStatements.text: The elements in the periodic table are arranged in order of atomic (proton) number and so that elements with similar properties are in columns, known as groups. The table is called a periodic table because similar properties occur at regular intervals.
Elements in the same group in the periodic table have the same number of electrons in their outer shell (outer electrons) and this gives them similar chemical properties.
Students should be able to:
explain how the position of an element in the periodic table is related to the arrangement of electrons in its atoms and hence to its atomic number
predict possible reactions and probable reactivity of elements from their positions in the periodic table.
Before the discovery of protons, neutrons and electrons, scientists attempted to classify the elements by arranging them in order of their atomic weights.
The early periodic tables were incomplete and some elements were placed in inappropriate groups if the strict order of atomic weights was followed.
Mendeleev overcame some of the problems by leaving gaps for elements that he thought had not been discovered and in some places changed the order based on atomic weights.
Elements with properties predicted by Mendeleev were discovered and filled the gaps. Knowledge of isotopes made it possible to explain why the order based on atomic weights was not always correct.
Students should be able to describe these steps in the development of the periodic table.
Elements that react to form positive ions are metals.
Elements that do not form positive ions are non-metals.
The majority of elements are metals. Metals are found to the left and towards the bottom of the periodic table. Non-metals are found towards the right and top of the periodic table.
Students should be able to:

explain the differences between metals and non-metals on the basis of their characteristic physical and chemical properties. This links to Group 0 , Group 1 , Group 7 and Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
explain how the atomic structure of metals and non-metals relates to their position in the periodic table
explain how the reactions of elements are related to the arrangement of electrons in their atoms and hence to their atomic number.

The elements in Group 0 of the periodic table are called the noble gases. They are unreactive and do not easily form molecules because their atoms have stable arrangements of electrons. The noble gases have eight electrons in their outer shell, except for helium, which has only two electrons.
The boiling points of the noble gases increase with increasing relative atomic mass (going down the group).
Students should be able to:
explain how properties of the elements in Group 0 depend on the outer shell of electrons of the atoms
predict properties from given trends down the group.
The elements in Group 1 of the periodic table are known as the alkali metals and have characteristic properties because of the single electron in their outer shell.
Students should be able to describe the reactions of the first three alkali metals with oxygen, chlorine and water.
In Group 1, the reactivity of the elements increases going down the group.
Students should be able to:
explain how properties of the elements in Group 1 depend on the outer shell of electrons of the atoms
predict properties from given trends down the group.

The elements in Group 7 of the periodic table are known as the halogens and have similar reactions because they all have seven electrons in their outer shell. The halogens are non-metals and consist of molecules made of pairs of atoms.
Students should be able to describe the nature of the compounds formed when chlorine, bromine and iodine react with metals and non-metals.
In Group 7, the further down the group an element is the higher its relative molecular mass, melting point and boiling point.
In Group 7, the reactivity of the elements decreases going down the group.
A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its salt.
Students should be able to:
explain how properties of the elements in Group 7 depend on the outer shell of electrons of the atoms
predict properties from given trends down the group.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to: (lead-in to the two bullets S04 and S05)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The line introduces two assessable bullets and holds no content of its own. It is honoured by assessing exactly those two skills and nothing further: q04 places an element from its electronic structure, q05 predicts reactivity from position. No question asks a student to recall the lead-in itself.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to: (lead-in to the three bullets S15, S16 and S17)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Honoured by assessing only the three bullets it introduces: metal against non-metal properties in q12, atomic structure and position in q13, and reactions traced back to electron arrangement in q14.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to: (lead-in to the two Group 0 bullets S21 and S22)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Honoured by assessing only those two bullets: the outer-shell explanation of unreactivity in q16 and prediction from a supplied trend in q18.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to: (lead-in to the two Group 1 bullets S27 and S28)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Honoured by assessing only those two bullets: the outer-shell explanation of the reactivity trend in q23 and prediction from a supplied trend in q22.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to: (lead-in to the two Group 7 bullets S35 and S36)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Honoured by assessing only those two bullets: the outer-shell explanation in q27 and prediction from a supplied trend in q26.

scopeNotes.statement: Reactions required are those of the first three alkali metals with oxygen, chlorine and water.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Questions on Group 1 reactions use only lithium, sodium and potassium, and only with water (q20), oxygen and chlorine (q21). Rubidium and caesium appear solely as prediction targets in q05 and q22, where the specification asks for prediction from trends rather than recall of reactions.

scopeNotes.statement: Compounds required are those formed when chlorine, bromine and iodine react with metals and non-metals.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: q25 uses chlorine with a metal and with a non-metal; q28 uses chlorine and bromine. Fluorine is never used as a reactant, and astatine appears only as a prediction target in q26.

scopeNotes.statement: Prediction of properties is from given trends down the group; recall of particular data values is not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: q18, q22 and q26 supply every measured value inside the stem and ask only for a prediction that continues the pattern. No question requires a student to remember a boiling point, a melting point or a density.

concepts.definition: The arrangement of all the elements in order of atomic (proton) number, set out so that elements with similar properties fall in the same column.
A column of the periodic table. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons and so have similar chemical properties.
A row of the periodic table. The period number equals the number of occupied electron shells in an atom of the element.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. It fixes the element's place in the periodic table.
The electrons in the highest occupied shell of an atom. Their number decides the group and controls the element's chemical reactions.
The repeating of similar properties at regular intervals along the order of elements, which is why the table is called periodic.
The mass measure used to order elements before subatomic particles were known; now called relative atomic mass.
Spaces left in his table for elements he believed had not yet been discovered, with properties predicted from the neighbouring elements.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, which is why atomic weight does not always rise with proton number.
An element that reacts to form positive ions. Metals lie to the left and towards the bottom of the periodic table.
An element that does not form positive ions. Non-metals lie towards the right and top of the periodic table.
An ion formed when an atom loses one or more electrons, leaving more protons than electrons.
The elements of Group 0. They are unreactive and do not easily form molecules because their atoms have stable electron arrangements.
An outer shell holding eight electrons, or two in the case of helium, so the atom has no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons.
Boiling points increase with increasing relative atomic mass, that is, going down the group.
The elements of Group 1. Their characteristic properties follow from the single electron in the outer shell of their atoms.
The alkaline compound produced, along with hydrogen, when a Group 1 metal reacts with water.
Reactivity increases going down the group, as the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost.
The elements of Group 7. They are non-metals with seven outer electrons whose atoms go about in pairs as molecules.
A molecule made of two atoms joined together, the form in which the halogen elements exist, such as Cl2 and Br2.
The ionic compound formed when a halogen reacts with a metal, such as sodium chloride or iron bromide.
The covalent compound formed when a halogen reacts with a non-metal, such as hydrogen chloride.
Reactivity decreases going down the group, as the outer shell is further from the nucleus and an electron is gained less easily.
A reaction in which a more reactive halogen takes the place of a less reactive halogen in an aqueous solution of its salt.

misconceptions.question: Does the group number tell you how many electron shells an atom has?
misconceptions.correct: The group number gives the number of outer electrons; the number of occupied shells gives the period.
misconceptions.misconception: The group number counts the shells, so 2,8,7 belongs in Group 3 because it has three shells.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Group and period are both position numbers and nothing in the words says which belongs to shells, so students attach the first number they meet to the first idea they meet.
misconceptions.correction: Read the structure twice: 2,8,7 has three occupied shells, so Period 3, and seven outer electrons, so Group 7.

misconceptions.question: Is the modern periodic table arranged in order of relative atomic mass?
misconceptions.correct: It is arranged in order of atomic (proton) number.
misconceptions.misconception: The table is ordered by relative atomic mass, the larger number printed in each box.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Relative atomic mass appears on every data sheet and usually does rise from left to right, and it genuinely was the ordering rule before protons were known.
misconceptions.correction: Check tellurium and iodine: mass falls but proton number rises, and the table follows proton number.

misconceptions.question: Why is the table called periodic?
misconceptions.correct: Because similar properties occur at regular intervals along the order of elements.
misconceptions.misconception: Because the table is revised from time to time as new elements are added.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Outside chemistry a periodical is something published at intervals in time, so the everyday meaning of the word is carried across.
misconceptions.correction: Periodic here describes the pattern in the properties, not the history of the table.

misconceptions.question: Do elements in the same group have the same number of electrons altogether?
misconceptions.correct: They have the same number of outer electrons, but different total numbers.
misconceptions.misconception: Elements in the same group are treated as identical - equal outer-electron counts and matching physical properties such as boiling point, melting point and reactivity - because they behave alike.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know a shared number causes the shared behaviour and reach for the only electron count they can name.
misconceptions.correction: Chlorine has 17 electrons and bromine 35; what they share is seven in the outer shell.

misconceptions.question: Does the number of neutrons fix an element's place in the table?
misconceptions.correct: The number of protons fixes the place; neutron number can vary within one element.
misconceptions.misconception: Elements are ordered by how many neutrons their atoms hold.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Protons and neutrons are taught together as the nuclear particles, so they get treated as interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: Isotopes of one element share a place in the table despite holding different numbers of neutrons.

misconceptions.question: Did Mendeleev arrange the elements by atomic number?
misconceptions.correct: He worked before protons were known and arranged them by atomic weight.
misconceptions.misconception: Mendeleev used atomic number, which is why his table came out right.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The modern rule is learned first, so it is read back into the history as though it had always been available.
misconceptions.correction: Protons were not discovered until after Mendeleev's table; he had only weights and properties to work with.

misconceptions.question: Why did Mendeleev leave gaps in his table?
misconceptions.correct: He left them for elements he believed had not yet been discovered.
misconceptions.misconception: The gaps mark places where no element can ever exist.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A gap looks like a permanent hole rather than a booking made for a guest who has not arrived.
misconceptions.correction: Elements with the properties he predicted were later found and filled those gaps.

misconceptions.question: What is different between two isotopes of one element?
misconceptions.correct: They have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Isotopes are atoms with different numbers of protons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Isotope is remembered simply as different atoms of the same element, without which particle actually differs.
misconceptions.correction: Change the protons and you change the element, so only the neutron count can differ between isotopes.

misconceptions.question: Were Mendeleev's changes to the weight order mistakes?
misconceptions.correct: He swapped some pairs so that elements fell in with others of similar properties, and isotopes later explained why.
misconceptions.misconception: The swaps were errors that modern chemists have since put back into weight order.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Following the data is taught as good practice, so deliberately departing from it looks like cheating.
misconceptions.correction: The modern table keeps his swaps, because ordering by proton number puts those pairs exactly where he placed them.

misconceptions.question: What kind of ion does a metal form?
misconceptions.correct: A metal reacts to form a positive ion by losing electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Metals form negative ions because they are heavy and hold electrons tightly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sign conventions are memorised without the electron-transfer picture, so the two signs get swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Losing negative electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion carries a positive charge.

misconceptions.question: Do non-metals form positive ions?
misconceptions.correct: They do not form positive ions; elements that do are metals.
misconceptions.misconception: Non-metals on the right form positive ions because they have many outer electrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Having lots of outer electrons sounds like having lots to give away.
misconceptions.correction: An atom with a nearly full outer shell gains electrons rather than losing them, so any ion it forms is negative.

misconceptions.question: Are most of the elements metals or non-metals?
misconceptions.correct: The majority of the elements are metals.
misconceptions.misconception: Most elements are non-metals, since the everyday non-metals are the familiar ones.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Oxygen, carbon, nitrogen and chlorine dominate school chemistry, so non-metals feel more numerous.
misconceptions.correction: Count the table: the whole centre, left and bottom are metals, and non-metals occupy only a small block at the top right.

misconceptions.question: Where in the periodic table are the metals found?
misconceptions.correct: To the left and towards the bottom.
misconceptions.misconception: Metals sit on the right of the table, near the heavier elements.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Left and right are learned as a bare fact with nothing to anchor them, so the pair is easy to invert.
misconceptions.correction: Sodium, magnesium and iron are all on the left or centre; the right-hand edge holds oxygen, chlorine and the noble gases.

misconceptions.question: Why are the noble gases unreactive?
misconceptions.correct: Their atoms have stable arrangements of electrons, so they have no tendency to gain, lose or share.
misconceptions.misconception: They are unreactive because their outer shell is empty.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Unreactive is heard as having nothing there, rather than as having nothing left to want.
misconceptions.correction: Argon is 2,8,8; the outer shell is as full as it can be, which is precisely why nothing happens.

misconceptions.question: Does every noble gas have eight outer electrons?
misconceptions.correct: All of them do except helium, which has only two.
misconceptions.misconception: Helium has eight outer electrons like the rest of Group 0.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule of eight is learned as universal, and helium's position at the top of the group hides its first-shell limit.
misconceptions.correction: Helium is simply 2: the first shell holds two electrons and is then complete.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the boiling points of the noble gases down the group?
misconceptions.correct: They increase with increasing relative atomic mass, that is, going down.
misconceptions.misconception: Boiling points fall down Group 0 because the gases get lighter.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Group 1 reactivity increases down the group and Group 7 reactivity decreases, so trend directions become a coin toss.
misconceptions.correction: Helium boils at about -269 C and radon well above -100 C: the values climb going down.

misconceptions.question: Do the noble gases exist as molecules?
misconceptions.correct: They do not easily form molecules; they exist as separate atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: Neon and argon go about as diatomic molecules like oxygen and chlorine.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most familiar gases in the laboratory are diatomic, so the pattern is over-generalised.
misconceptions.correction: A stable outer shell gives no reason to bond, so noble gas atoms stay single.

misconceptions.question: What happens to reactivity going down Group 1?
misconceptions.correct: Reactivity increases going down the group.
misconceptions.misconception: The alkali metals become less reactive further down, as the atoms are heavier.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Heavier is taken to mean more sluggish, and the Group 7 trend is remembered in place of the Group 1 one.
misconceptions.correction: Lithium fizzes, sodium melts into a ball and potassium ignites: the reaction gets more violent going down.

misconceptions.question: What does a Group 1 atom do with its outer electron?
misconceptions.correct: It loses that single electron to form an ion with a 1+ charge.
misconceptions.misconception: A Group 1 atom gains seven electrons to complete its outer shell.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule remembered is fill the outer shell, and gaining seven is the only way to do that from one.
misconceptions.correction: Losing one electron leaves a full shell underneath, which takes far less energy than gaining seven.

misconceptions.question: What is made when a Group 1 metal reacts with water?
misconceptions.correct: A metal hydroxide and hydrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: The wrong metal compound is given as the product: an oxide (or another salt such as a chloride) plus a gas instead of the hydroxide when a metal reacts with water, or a hydroxide instead of the oxide when the metal burns in oxygen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Oxide is the first metal-and-oxygen compound met, and the oxygen in water makes it look like the obvious product.
misconceptions.correction: The solution turns universal indicator purple because a soluble hydroxide, not an oxide, has been made.

misconceptions.question: Why does reactivity increase down Group 1?
misconceptions.correct: The outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily.
misconceptions.misconception: Reactivity rises because atoms further down have more electrons available to give away.
misconceptions.whyItArises: More electrons sounds like more to react with, and the fact that only one electron is lost is overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: Every Group 1 atom loses exactly one electron; what changes is how tightly that one is held.

misconceptions.question: In what form does chlorine exist as an element?
misconceptions.correct: As Cl2 molecules, pairs of atoms joined together.
misconceptions.misconception: Chlorine gas is made of single chlorine atoms.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The symbol Cl is what appears in the data sheet, so the element is pictured as lone atoms.
misconceptions.correction: The halogens all consist of molecules made of pairs of atoms, written Cl2, Br2 and I2.

misconceptions.question: What happens to reactivity going down Group 7?
misconceptions.correct: Reactivity decreases going down the group.
misconceptions.misconception: The halogens get more reactive further down, in the same way as Group 1.
misconceptions.whyItArises: One reactivity trend is learned and then applied to both groups without asking whether electrons are gained or lost.
misconceptions.correction: Chlorine displaces bromine from potassium bromide, and bromine displaces iodine, so reactivity falls going down.

misconceptions.question: What sort of compound forms when a halogen reacts with a metal?
misconceptions.correct: An ionic compound, a metal halide such as sodium chloride.
misconceptions.misconception: Halogens are non-metals, so they form covalent (molecular) compounds with everything they react with; a halogen reacting with a metal gives molecules, not an ionic metal halide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Halogens are non-metals themselves, so students expect them to share electrons with whatever they meet.
misconceptions.correction: Metal plus non-metal transfers electrons and gives ions; two non-metals share and give molecules.

misconceptions.question: What happens to melting and boiling points down Group 7?
misconceptions.correct: They increase, as relative molecular mass increases down the group.
misconceptions.misconception: Melting points fall down Group 7 because the elements grow less reactive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Reactivity falls down the group, so every trend is assumed to fall with it.
misconceptions.correction: Chlorine is a gas, bromine a liquid and iodine a solid at room temperature: the points climb going down.

misconceptions.question: Which halogen displaces which from a solution of a salt?
misconceptions.correct: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from an aqueous solution of its salt.
misconceptions.misconception: Iodine displaces chlorine because iodine atoms are larger and heavier.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Bigger is read as stronger, and the direction of the reactivity trend in Group 7 is forgotten.
misconceptions.correction: Add chlorine to potassium bromide and the solution turns orange as bromine is set free; the reverse does nothing.

misconceptions.question: Which elements have similar properties, those in a row or those in a column?
misconceptions.correct: Those in the same column, that is, the same group.
misconceptions.misconception: Elements next to each other in a period behave alike because they are neighbours.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Nearness on the page is taken to mean chemical likeness, and rows are read before columns.
misconceptions.correction: Sodium and magnesium are neighbours yet behave very differently; sodium and potassium are a row apart and behave alike.

misconceptions.question: What is the formula of the compound sodium makes with chlorine?
misconceptions.correct: NaCl, because one sodium ion carries 1+ and one chloride ion carries 1-.
misconceptions.misconception: The formula is NaCl2, since chlorine is Cl2 as an element.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The diatomic formula of the element is carried over into the compound unchanged.
misconceptions.correction: The Cl-Cl bond breaks in the reaction, and charges of 1+ and 1- balance one to one.

misconceptions.question: Why were some elements in the wrong groups in early tables?
misconceptions.correct: Strict order of atomic weights placed a few elements with others they did not resemble.
misconceptions.misconception: Their atomic weights had simply been measured wrongly, and better apparatus fixed the table.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A rule that gives a wrong answer is assumed to have been applied to faulty data rather than to be the wrong rule.
misconceptions.correction: The weights were about right; the rule itself was the problem, as isotopes later showed.

misconceptions.question: What did knowledge of isotopes contribute to the periodic table?
misconceptions.correct: It explained why an order based on atomic weights is not always correct.
misconceptions.misconception: It allowed atomic weights to be measured more precisely, which fixed the order.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Isotopes are associated with mass, so their role is assumed to be about better numbers rather than about a better rule.
misconceptions.correction: Argon is heavier than potassium because of its isotope mixture, yet it has fewer protons, so proton number is the sounder rule.

mcqs.stem: In the modern periodic table the elements are set out one after another in order of which quantity?

options.text: Atomic (proton) number, going up by one at each step
options.rationale: The specification states that the elements are arranged in order of atomic (proton) number, and that number climbs by one at every step.

options.text: Relative atomic mass, the larger number in each box
options.rationale: Relative atomic mass is printed on every data sheet and usually does rise left to right, and it was genuinely the old ordering rule.

options.text: The number of occupied electron shells it has
options.rationale: A student holding m01 (group counts shells) assumes the whole table is sequenced by shell count.

options.text: Number of neutrons in the nucleus of an atom
options.rationale: Protons and neutrons are learned together as nuclear particles and get treated as interchangeable.

mcqs.stem: Why is the table of the elements described as periodic?

options.text: Because the table is revised at regular periods as new elements appear
options.rationale: Outside chemistry a periodical is something issued at intervals in time, and that everyday meaning is carried across.

options.text: Because elements with similar properties recur at regular intervals
options.rationale: The specification says the table is called periodic because similar properties occur at regular intervals along it.

options.text: Because every row repeats the properties of the row above it
options.rationale: Rows are read before columns, so the repetition is expected to run across a period rather than down a group.

options.text: Because each element repeats the electron count before it
options.rationale: Something must repeat for the name to make sense, and total electron count is the count students can name.

mcqs.stem: Chlorine and bromine are both in Group 7 and react in similar ways. What do atoms of these two elements share?

options.text: The same total number of electrons in the whole atom
options.rationale: A shared number is known to cause the shared behaviour, and total electron count is the first count reached for.

options.text: The same number of occupied shells in the atom
options.rationale: Group and period get swapped, so the group number is read as a count of shells.

options.text: The same number of outer electrons in an atom
options.rationale: Elements in one group have the same number of outer electrons, and that is what gives them similar chemical properties.

options.text: The same number of neutrons in the nucleus
options.rationale: Nuclear particles are treated as the thing that decides position, so neutrons are offered as the shared feature.

mcqs.stem: An atom of element X has the electronic structure 2,8,7. Where in the periodic table is X found?

options.text: Group 3 and Period 7, reading its three occupied shells
options.rationale: The two position numbers are attached the wrong way round, so shells are counted as the group.

options.text: Group 17 and Period 3, counting all the electrons
options.rationale: Adding the electrons up gives 17, and that total is offered as the group instead of the outer count.

options.text: Group 3 and Period 3, since the shell count gives both
options.rationale: The outer count is correctly read as the group, then used again for the period, which needs the number of shells.

options.text: Group 7 and Period 3, from seven outer electrons
options.rationale: Seven electrons in the outer shell places X in Group 7, and three occupied shells places it in Period 3.

mcqs.stem: Rubidium lies below potassium in Group 1. From its position, what can be predicted about its reaction with water?

options.text: It reacts less vigorously than potassium, being a heavier metal
options.rationale: Heavier is read as more sluggish, and the falling Group 7 trend is applied to Group 1 by mistake.

options.text: It reacts more vigorously than potassium, giving off hydrogen gas
options.rationale: Reactivity increases down Group 1, so rubidium reacts more vigorously than potassium and gives rubidium hydroxide and hydrogen.

options.text: It reacts to give rubidium oxide along with hydrogen gas
options.rationale: Oxide is the first metal-oxygen compound met, and the oxygen in water makes it look like the product.

options.text: It reacts much like strontium, its neighbour in that period
options.rationale: Neighbours on the page are assumed to be chemically alike, but likeness runs down groups, not along periods.

mcqs.stem: Before protons, neutrons and electrons were discovered, how did scientists attempt to classify the elements?

options.text: By arranging them in order of the atomic number
options.rationale: The modern rule is learned first and read back into a period when it was not yet available.

options.text: By arranging them in order of their outer electron counts
options.rationale: Electrons had not been discovered either, but the modern explanation of groups is applied to the early work anyway.

options.text: By arranging them in order of their atomic weights
options.rationale: The specification states that before those particles were known, scientists classified elements by ordering them by atomic weight.

options.text: By arranging them in order of their neutron count
options.rationale: Neutrons are treated as interchangeable with protons, so they are offered as an early ordering rule.

mcqs.stem: What problem arose in the early periodic tables when the strict order of atomic weights was followed?

options.text: Faulty weight values scattered elements far from their true partners
options.rationale: If the weights were mismeasured (m29), elements would be pushed away from the families they belong with.

options.text: The atomic weights themselves had all been measured wrongly
options.rationale: A rule that gives a wrong answer is assumed to have had faulty data rather than to be the wrong rule.

options.text: Permanent gaps appeared that no element could ever fill
options.rationale: Holding m07 (gaps are permanent holes), the student sees weight-ordering as leaving unfillable blanks.

options.text: Some elements were placed in groups they did not belong in
options.rationale: The specification states that early tables were incomplete and that strict weight order put some elements in inappropriate groups.

mcqs.stem: Mendeleev left gaps in his periodic table. Why did he do this?

options.text: He expected undiscovered elements to fill them
options.rationale: Mendeleev overcame some of the problems by leaving gaps for elements he thought had not yet been discovered.

options.text: He believed that no element could ever exist there
options.rationale: A gap looks like a permanent hole rather than a place reserved for something still to come.

options.text: He thought those places in nature were forever empty
options.rationale: With m07 the student believes gaps mark spots where no element can ever exist.

options.text: He was unsure of several measured atomic weights
options.rationale: Doubt about the data is a plausible motive, but the gaps stood for missing elements, not for doubtful numbers.

mcqs.stem: Knowledge of isotopes helped chemists understand the periodic table. What exactly did it explain?

options.text: Why atomic weights could be measured far more precisely
options.rationale: Isotopes are associated with mass, so their role is assumed to be about better numbers rather than a better rule.

options.text: Why two atoms of one element hold different protons
options.rationale: Isotope is remembered as different atoms of one element without which particle actually differs.

options.text: Why an order based on atomic weights is not always correct
options.rationale: Isotope mixtures mean atomic weight does not always rise with proton number, which explains the pairs Mendeleev had to swap.

options.text: Why Mendeleev's swapped pairs were mistakes after all
options.rationale: Departing from the data looks like cheating, but the modern table keeps every one of those swaps.

mcqs.stem: Sodium reacts to form Na+ ions and sulfur does not form positive ions. What does this tell you about them?

options.text: Sodium is a non-metal and sulfur is a metal
options.rationale: The two signs are simply swapped, which turns the classification upside down.

options.text: Sodium must be a non-metal, because it forms a positive ion
options.rationale: Taking part in a reaction is confused with the specific behaviour of forming positive ions.

options.text: Both are non-metals, since neither formed a negative ion
options.rationale: Under m10 (metals form negative ions), neither sodium nor sulfur made a negative ion, so both look non-metal.

options.text: Sodium is a metal and sulfur is a non-metal element
options.rationale: Elements that react to form positive ions are metals; elements that do not form positive ions are non-metals.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly describes where metals and non-metals sit in the periodic table?

options.text: Most elements are metals, on the left and lower down
options.rationale: The majority of elements are metals, found to the left and towards the bottom, with non-metals towards the right and top.

options.text: Most elements are metals, on the right near the top
options.rationale: The classification is right but left and right are inverted, a pair learned as a bare fact with nothing to anchor it.

options.text: Most elements are non-metals, on the left and lower down
options.rationale: Oxygen, carbon and chlorine dominate school chemistry, so non-metals feel like the larger group.

options.text: Most elements are non-metals, over on the right
options.rationale: Believing non-metals dominate (m12), the student places the majority on the familiar right-hand side.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of properties would you expect a typical metal to show, in contrast to a typical non-metal?

options.text: A poor conductor of heat that forms negative ions
options.rationale: The sign of the ion is inverted and the conduction property is inverted with it.

options.text: A good heat conductor that forms positive ions
options.rationale: Metals conduct heat and electricity well and react to form positive ions; typical non-metals do neither.

options.text: A good conductor of heat, yet it forms negative ions
options.rationale: The physical property is right but the ion charge is inverted, the commonest single slip here.

options.text: A poor conductor of heat which forms positive ions
options.rationale: The ion charge is right but the physical property has been taken from a non-metal such as sulfur.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium has the electronic structure 2,8,2. How does this relate to its position in the periodic table?

options.text: Two outer electrons put it in Group 2, on the right
options.rationale: The group is read correctly but the metal side of the table is placed on the wrong edge.

options.text: Two outer electrons put it in Group 2, identical to calcium
options.rationale: Inner electrons are counted instead of outer ones, which is not what the group number records.

options.text: Two outer electrons make it a non-metal in Group 2
options.rationale: Having only two outer electrons is read as being close to a non-metal rather than as being easy to lose.

options.text: Two outer electrons put it in Group 2, among the metals
options.rationale: Two outer electrons place magnesium in Group 2, on the left of the table, where elements lose electrons to form positive ions.

mcqs.stem: Why does magnesium react to form Mg2+ ions while chlorine reacts to form Cl- ions?

options.text: Magnesium loses its two outer electrons; chlorine gains one
options.rationale: Reactions follow the arrangement of electrons: an atom with few outer electrons loses them, one with a nearly full shell gains.

options.text: Magnesium gains six electrons and chlorine loses seven
options.rationale: Fill the outer shell is remembered as the rule, and gaining or losing whatever it takes is applied blindly.

options.text: Magnesium has more protons than chlorine has in total
options.rationale: Charge on the ion is traced to nuclear particles rather than to the electrons actually transferred.

options.text: Magnesium has outer electrons it readily gives away
options.rationale: With m21 the student thinks having electrons to give away is why magnesium loses them to form Mg2+.

mcqs.stem: The noble gases in Group 0 are unreactive. Which statement explains this and describes their outer shells?

options.text: Their outer shells are empty, so there is nothing left to react
options.rationale: Unreactive is heard as having nothing there rather than as having nothing left to want.

options.text: Their arrangements are stable, eight outer but two in helium
options.rationale: Noble gases are unreactive because their atoms have stable electron arrangements: eight outer electrons, or two in helium.

options.text: Every one of them holds exactly eight electrons in the outer shell
options.rationale: The rule of eight is treated as universal, and helium's two-electron first shell is overlooked.

options.text: They travel as pairs, so their bonds are already used
options.rationale: Believing noble gases are diatomic (m17), the student thinks their bonds are already committed.

mcqs.stem: Argon has the electronic structure 2,8,8. Why does argon not easily form molecules?

options.text: It has already shared its electrons within a pair
options.rationale: With m17 the student thinks argon exists as a bonded pair, its electrons already shared.

options.text: Its atoms already exist joined together in pairs
options.rationale: Most familiar laboratory gases are diatomic, so the pattern is over-generalised to Group 0.

options.text: Its outer shell is stable, so it need not share
options.rationale: With a stable outer arrangement, argon has no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons, so it does not easily form molecules.

options.text: Its outer shell has no electrons available to share
options.rationale: An unreactive atom is pictured as an empty one, when in fact its outer shell is complete.

mcqs.stem: What happens to the boiling points of the noble gases as relative atomic mass increases down Group 0?

options.text: They increase steadily going further down the group
options.rationale: The specification states that the boiling points of the noble gases increase with increasing relative atomic mass.

options.text: They decrease as the gases become lighter down it
options.rationale: Trend directions become a coin toss once Group 1 and Group 7 are found to run opposite ways.

options.text: They stay the same, as these gases are stable
options.rationale: Chemical similarity within a group is over-extended to physical properties, which do change down it.

options.text: They fall sharply, halving with each step down
options.rationale: Holding m16, the student predicts boiling points fall down the group, here dropping steeply.

mcqs.stem: Boiling points in Group 0 are helium -269 C, neon -246 C, argon -186 C. Predict the boiling point of krypton.

options.text: Below -269 C, continuing past helium at the top
options.rationale: The trend is read the wrong way down the group, so the prediction runs off the cold end.

options.text: About -153 C, carrying the rise further down
options.rationale: Boiling points increase down Group 0, so krypton, below argon, must boil at a higher temperature than -186 C.

options.text: About -230 C, falling below argon down the group
options.rationale: With m16 the student expects boiling points to keep falling, so krypton sits below argon.

options.text: About -246 C, the same value as neon shows
options.rationale: Members of a group are expected to share physical values, but only chemical behaviour is similar.

mcqs.stem: The Group 1 elements are known as the alkali metals. Which feature of their atoms gives them their characteristic properties?

options.text: Their atoms each hold just a single occupied electron shell
options.rationale: The group number is read as a count of shells, so Group 1 is taken to mean one shell.

options.text: Their atoms each need a single electron more to fill a shell
options.rationale: Fill the outer shell is applied without checking whether one is missing or one is spare.

options.text: Their atoms each have a single electron in the outer shell
options.rationale: Group 1 elements have characteristic properties because of the single electron in their outer shell.

options.text: Their atoms each have a single proton in the nucleus
options.rationale: The group number is attached to nuclear particles instead of to the outer electrons.

mcqs.stem: A small piece of potassium is dropped onto water. What are the products of the reaction?

options.text: Potassium oxide and hydrogen gas are both formed
options.rationale: Oxide is the first metal-oxygen compound met, and the oxygen in water makes it look like the product.

options.text: Potassium chloride and hydrogen gas are given off
options.rationale: The chlorine reaction is recalled in place of the water one, since both give a white solid product.

options.text: Potassium oxide and oxygen gas are given off
options.rationale: Both parts of water are assumed to be released, but the hydrogen is what bubbles off.

options.text: Potassium hydroxide and hydrogen gas form
options.rationale: A Group 1 metal reacts with water to give a metal hydroxide and hydrogen: 2K + 2H2O gives 2KOH + H2.

mcqs.stem: Lithium is burned in oxygen, and separately sodium is burned in chlorine. What are the two products?

options.text: Lithium oxide and covalent sodium chloride molecules
options.rationale: The halogen is a non-metal, so students expect it to share electrons with whatever it meets.

options.text: Lithium oxide, Li2O, and sodium chloride, NaCl, are made
options.rationale: Group 1 metals burn in oxygen to give the metal oxide and in chlorine to give the metal chloride: 4Li + O2 gives 2Li2O.

options.text: Lithium hydroxide and sodium chloride solution
options.rationale: The products of the water reaction are transferred to the reactions with oxygen and chlorine.

options.text: Lithium oxide, LiO, plus sodium chloride, NaCl2
options.rationale: The diatomic formulas of the elements are carried into the compounds instead of balancing the ion charges.

mcqs.stem: Lithium reacts steadily with water, sodium melts into a ball and potassium bursts into flame. Predict how caesium behaves.

options.text: Less vigorously than lithium, being the heaviest metal here
options.rationale: Heavier is read as more sluggish, so the trend is run backwards up the group.

options.text: About the same as potassium, as both are in Group 1
options.rationale: Membership of one group is taken to mean identical behaviour rather than similar behaviour.

options.text: Even more vigorously than potassium, reacting explosively
options.rationale: Reactivity increases down Group 1, so caesium, well below potassium, reacts more violently still.

options.text: Steadily, because its outer electron is held tightly
options.rationale: The outer electron of a large atom is assumed to be gripped harder, when it is in fact held more loosely.

mcqs.stem: Why does the reactivity of the Group 1 metals increase going down the group?

options.text: Atoms lower down have many more electrons to give away
options.rationale: More electrons sounds like more to react with, though every Group 1 atom loses exactly one.

options.text: Atoms lower down have more protons pulling on the shell
options.rationale: Extra protons are counted while the extra shells that separate them from the outer electron are ignored.

options.text: Atoms lower down need to gain fewer electrons
options.rationale: The rule fill the outer shell is applied to a metal that in fact empties its outer shell.

options.text: The outer electron is further out, so easily lost
options.rationale: Going down the group the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so the attraction is weaker and it is lost more easily.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly describes the elements of Group 7, the halogens?

options.text: Non-metals with seven outer electrons, found as pairs
options.rationale: The halogens are non-metals with seven electrons in the outer shell, and they consist of molecules made of pairs of atoms.

options.text: Non-metals with seven outer electrons, existing as atoms
options.rationale: The symbol Cl in the data sheet is taken as the form of the element, so the pairing is missed.

options.text: Metals with seven outer electrons, going about in pairs
options.rationale: Having many outer electrons is read as having plenty to give away, which sounds metallic.

options.text: Non-metals with seven electron shells, joined in pairs
options.rationale: The group number is read as a count of shells rather than of outer electrons.

mcqs.stem: Chlorine reacts with sodium, and separately with hydrogen. What kinds of compound are formed?

options.text: An ionic compound with sodium, and ions with hydrogen too
options.rationale: Chlorine is treated as always producing ions, and the non-metal partner is not taken into account.

options.text: A covalent compound with sodium, and ions with hydrogen
options.rationale: The two cases are inverted: the halogen being a non-metal is taken to force sharing with the metal.

options.text: An ionic compound with sodium, and a molecule with hydrogen
options.rationale: A halogen with a metal gives an ionic metal halide, NaCl; with a non-metal it gives a covalent molecule, HCl.

options.text: A covalent compound in both, since chlorine is a non-metal
options.rationale: One rule is applied to both partners, but a metal and a non-metal transfer electrons rather than sharing them.

mcqs.stem: Melting points in Group 7 are chlorine -101 C, bromine -7 C, iodine 114 C. Predict the melting point of astatine.

options.text: About -150 C, since reactivity falls down the group
options.rationale: Falling reactivity is assumed to drag every other property down with it.

options.text: About -90 C, dropping since reactivity falls
options.rationale: Holding m25 (melting points fall as reactivity falls), the student predicts a low value for astatine.

options.text: About 114 C, matching iodine in the group
options.rationale: Members of a group are expected to share physical values, but only chemical behaviour is similar.

options.text: About 300 C, continuing the rise on below iodine
options.rationale: Melting and boiling points increase down Group 7 as relative molecular mass increases, so astatine melts above iodine.

mcqs.stem: Why does the reactivity of the halogens decrease going down Group 7?

options.text: The outer shell is further out, so gaining one is harder
options.rationale: Going down the group the outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so an electron is attracted and gained less easily.

options.text: Larger atoms are heavier, so they must react more sluggishly
options.rationale: Mass is used as the explanation, but what matters is how strongly an incoming electron is attracted.

options.text: Extra shells lower down leave fewer outer electrons exposed
options.rationale: Conflating shells with outer electrons (m01), the student thinks added shells reduce the electrons available.

options.text: Atoms lower down lose their outer electrons more easily
options.rationale: The Group 1 explanation is transferred wholesale to elements that gain an electron instead.

mcqs.stem: Chlorine solution is added to colourless potassium bromide solution. What is observed, and why?

options.text: No change, as bromine is the more reactive halogen
options.rationale: The reactivity trend is inverted, so the larger halogen is taken to be the stronger one.

options.text: It turns orange, as bromine has been displaced
options.rationale: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromine from the solution of its salt: Cl2 + 2KBr gives 2KCl + Br2.

options.text: It turns orange as bromine displaces the chlorine
options.rationale: Holding m26 (larger, heavier halogen is more reactive), the student has bromine displace chlorine.

options.text: No change, since both elements sit in the same group
options.rationale: Sharing a group is taken to mean equal reactivity, but reactivity falls steadily down Group 7.

mcqs.stem: An atom of element Z has 15 protons. Where in the periodic table is Z found?

options.text: Group 5 and Period 3, from five outer electrons
options.rationale: 15 protons means 15 electrons, arranged 2,8,5. Five outer electrons give Group 5 and three occupied shells give Period 3.

options.text: Group 3 and Period 5, counting its three shells
options.rationale: The two position numbers are attached the wrong way round, so the shells are counted as the group.

options.text: Group 15 and Period 3, adding all its electrons
options.rationale: All 15 electrons are totalled and offered as the group, but the group records only the outer ones.

options.text: Group 5 and Period 5, both from the outer shell
options.rationale: The outer count correctly gives the group, then is used again for the period, which needs the number of shells.

mcqs.stem: An atom of element Q has 19 protons. What does an atom of Q do when it reacts?

options.text: Loses one electron to form a 1+ ion
options.rationale: 19 protons means 19 electrons, arranged 2,8,8,1. The single outer electron is lost, so Q is a metal forming a 1+ ion.

options.text: Loses its outer electron, giving a 1- ion
options.rationale: The electron transfer is right but the sign is swapped; losing a negative electron leaves a positive ion.

options.text: Gains seven electrons to form a 7- ion
options.rationale: Fill the outer shell is remembered as the rule, and gaining seven is the only way to do that from one.

options.text: Loses four electrons to make a 4+ ion
options.rationale: The four occupied shells of 2,8,8,1 are read as the group number, so four electrons are taken to be lost.
